rounds.text: Susan Electricals India Ltd demonstrates extraordinary capital efficiency, evidenced by a phenomenal ROE of 64.6% and a ROCE of 37.0%, both vastly outperforming sector benchmarks [E8, E9, E11, E12]. This operational excellence drives hyper-growth, with compounded sales surging 99% over the trailing twelve months and profit growth hitting an astonishing 223% over the same period [E15, E18]. Fundamental strength is further validated by a five-year profit CAGR of 196% and a consistent multi-year operating margin expansion from 2% to 12% [E16, E22, E43]. Valued at a P/E of just 22.3x alongside a discounted cash flow intrinsic value of Rs 360 per share, the market significantly underestimates these robust fundamentals [E1, E35, E36]. Additionally, the business benefits from a strong macro backdrop with the Capital Goods sector in a clear tailwind [E48, E49]. Conceded: institutional money flow reads negative with a holding change of -13.34 percentage points, and operating cash flow is negative at Rs -10 Cr for Mar 2026 [E26, E34].

Despite seemingly impressive top-line growth, Susan Electricals India Ltd conceals severe financial and structural risks beneath its reported earnings [E18]. Most alarming is the company's complete detachment between accounting profits and actual cash generation, evidenced by a cash conversion of -0.56x and a negative operating cash flow of Rs -10 Cr, which further deepened free cash flow to a negative Rs -14 Cr in March 2026 [E25, E26, E27]. This cash drain forces the company to aggressively ramp up its debt, pushing borrowings to Rs 67 Cr and driving the debt-to-equity ratio to a precarious 1.72x where liabilities firmly exceed net worth [E28, E29]. Compounding these balance sheet vulnerabilities, institutional confidence has dramatically evaporated, highlighted by domestic institutions slashing their holdings by 11.34 percentage points and foreign institutions reducing theirs by 2.00 percentage points, resulting in a severe negative money flow signal [E32, E33, E34]. Furthermore, valuation multiples such as the P/E ratio reaching 31.63x and EV/EBITDA hitting 14.56x sit notably above sector benchmarks, exposing the equity to a harsh re-pricing if momentum stalls [E5, E10]. Conceded: the company demonstrates exceptional historical return metrics with a 5-year compounded profit growth of 196% and a 5-year median ROE of 52% [E16, E19].

Conceded: [E25, E26, E27]. While cash flows are temporarily negative and borrowings have risen to Rs 67 Cr resulting in a 1.72x debt-to-equity ratio [E28, E29], the bear exaggerates valuation risks by ignoring that filed statements place the P/E at a modest 22.3x [E1]. The company boasts exceptional profitability and capital efficiency, with ROE reaching 64.6% and ROCE hitting 37.0% [E12, E11], completely dwarfing sector benchmarks of 10.87% and 12.93% [E8, E9]. Furthermore, the bear's claim of high valuation overlooks the quantitative DCF model which places intrinsic value at Rs 360 against the market price of Rs 275 [E35], granting a healthy 23.6% margin of safety [E36]. The reverse DCF confirms that today's price prices in only 14.3% earnings growth, which is easily cleared by the company's historical 5-year profit growth of 196% [E37, E16]. Finally, the institutional outflow [E32, E33, E34] occurs against a robust macroeconomic backdrop where the Capital Goods sector sits firmly in a tailwind with a score of +0.68 [E48, E49].

Conceded: [E1]. The bull relies on a filed statements P/E of 22.3x [E1], but ignores that key-ratios data places the actual P/E significantly higher at 31.63x against a sector benchmark of 22.4x, alongside an elevated EV/EBITDA of 14.56x versus the sector's 12.66x [E5, E10]. While the bull celebrates high returns on equity and capital employed [E11, E12], these headline figures completely disconnect from cash generation as operating cash flow turned negative to Rs -10 Cr and free cash flow dropped to Rs -14 Cr in March 2026, dragging cash conversion down to -0.56x [E25, E26, E27]. This aggressive growth is entirely debt-funded rather than internally generated, evidenced by borrowings climbing to Rs 67 Cr and driving the debt-to-equity ratio to a risky 1.72x where debt exceeds net worth [E28, E29]. Furthermore, dismissing the massive institutional exodus as irrelevant is dangerous, given that foreign and domestic institutions dumped their holdings, causing a sharp negative money flow of -13.34 percentage points between June and September 2026 [E32, E33, E34]. Finally, the bull's reliance on DCF models and sector tailwinds [E35, E37, E48] cannot mask the fundamental deterioration of balance sheet leverage and non-existent dividend yield of 0.00% [E3, E28].
